rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Solve basic, direct current, electronic problems involving resistance, current, voltage, and power, as applied to both simple and complex combinations of series and/or parallel circuit components, comprised of resistors, capacitors and coils, in a given network configuration.
Diagram and discuss the relationship between electricity and magnetism as related to a DC permanent magnet motor, a solenoid or an electromechanical relay.
Describe and contrast the construction, operation, and purpose of resistors, potentiometers, switches, fuses, relays, and batteries.
objectives: Apply Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Voltage and Current Laws, and other foundational electrical principles in the analysis of circuits.
Master the fundamentals of voltage, current, resistance, and power in DC circuits.
Utilize network theorems like Thevenin’s and Norton’s for simplifying and solving circuits.
Conduct experiments and interpret results with standard electrical measurement tools to verify theoretical predictions.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following activities:

rows.title: Fundamentals of Tooling and Test Equipment
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Recognize, identify, and describe the functions of the major parts of industrial tools, including hand and power tools.
Recognize, identify, and describe the functions of test equipment.
Demonstrate knowledge the methods and tools used to resolve problems representative of maintenance environments.
Properly use personal protective equipment (safety goggles, hard hat, and personal fall protection) used in conjunction with hand and power tools.
Describe and demonstrate proper maintenance of hand and power tools.

rows.title: Industrial Wiring and Controls
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate competence in the planning, layout, documenting, wiring, testing, commissioning, maintaining, and troubleshooting electrical circuits based on schematic blue-prints, using safe and accurate methods, appropriate components, tools, wire, and ancillary devices.
objectives: Explain the various control strategies of starting industrial three-phase AC induction motors.
Design and explain an Electrical ladder diagram that will display the proper usage of switches, relays, timers, contactors, motor-starters, or other devices.
Design a Ladder-Logic Diagram, wire it and demonstrate the proper operations of a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) after programming it for a required behavior.
Troubleshoot and document repairs needed to correct a fault cause production-line delays.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following activities:

rows.title: Survey of Electronics
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate quantitative measurement of electrical circuit parameters in direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC) series, parallel, and series parallel circuits.
Draw a schematic depicting the proper connection of various electronic components in a given circuit configuration.
Appropriately and accurately analyze DC and AC circuits using Ohm's, Watt's and Kirchhoff's Law calculations.

Demonstrate the operation of electronic lab equipment to test components and circuits by properly connecting and operating the following standard test equipment: power supplies, function generators, ammeters, voltmeters, ohmmeters, analog and digital multimeters, oscilloscopes, and bridges.
objectives: Read and write schematic symbols that accurately depict the relationship of interconnections within a given circuit design.
Measure DC and AC parameters of a given circuit accurately.
Perform appropriate and accurate calculations to solve for unknowns in a given electrical or electronic circuit, choosing the proper formulas.
Understand electrical and electronic theories, devices, and circuit applications.

rows.title: Digital Techniques
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate competence with digital gates and systems, using truth-tables, Boolean Algebra, number systems, logic simplification, analysis, and design.
objectives: Demonstrate the operation of electronic lab equipment to test digital components and circuits by properly connecting and operating the following standard test equipment: logic probles, logic analyzers, power supplies, function generators, ammeters, voltmeters, ohmmeters, digital multimeters, and oscilloscopes.
Convert between the binary and decimal number systems and recognize the most commonly used binary codes.
Explain the operation of digital logic gates.
Identify the more commonly used integrated circuit families used in digital equipment and discuss their operation and characteristics.
Use Boolean algebra to express logic operations and minimize logic circuits in design.
Discuss the operation and application of counters, shift registers, and other sequential and combinational logic circuits.

rows.title: Introduction to the Electrical Trades and Construction Safety
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Perform a variety of measurements, and apply math, to properly solve word problems involving decimals and fractions, English and Metric units, conversions, and then use those solutions to demonstrate the appropriate application of industry standard, electrical tools and materials.

Research and cite the appropriate OSHA (CFR 1926/1910) standards in establishing safe construction site work practices, while listing hazards associated with energized electrical systems, along with demonstrating safe practices to deal with each, including Lock-Out, Tag-Out, and the safe use of motorized tools and platform lifts.
Demonstrate, while explaining, basic first aid and Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) techniques to use following accidents, including substance abuse emergencies.

rows.title: Digital Logic Circuits, Conductor Characteristics, Applications, and National Electric Code (NEC)
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

Draw a wiring diagram showing a 480/120 volt and 240/120 volt control transformer connection configuration; wire each, and test it, demonstrating competency with a variety of test instruments that are common in industry.

Demonstrate knowledge of the electrical industry hierarchy and the various factors needed to design, bid, organize and build an electrical project, including the knowledge of leadership and human motivational needs.

Correctly answer questions about the operation and installation requirements for intrusion detector sensors; and demonstrate knowledge of security systems by installing, testing, and troubleshooting secretly-sabotaged security equipment.

Analyze basic theory of data transmission and protocols.
Explain the use of basic wiring methods and fastening devices.
Analyze and select electrical conductors for various environmental and load conditions.
Identify, select and install pic, coaxial, and fiber optic cable per job specifications.

rows.title: Survey of Black Thought
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Critically analyze and articulate concepts of Black thought through an ethnic studies lens, engaging topics including, but not limited to, race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethnocentrism, Eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, and anti-racism as it relates to Black thinkers and philosophy.

Apply theories of Black thought to describe critical events in the histories, cultures, and intellectual traditions, with special focus on the lived experiences and social struggles of African Americans, emphasizing agency, identity formation, and group-afﬁrmation in response to Eurocentric approaches and white supremacist narratives.

Critically analyze the intersection of race, ethnicity, and gender with other forms of difference affected by hierarchy and oppression, such as class, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, and/or age, using the frameworks and theories of Black Thought scholars.

Describe how struggle, resistance, social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced by communities of color are relevant to current, historical, and structural issues as they relate to Black thought, both in the United States and in the broader African Diaspora.

Demonstrate active engagement with anti-racist, anti-colonial, anti-imperial thought, issues, practices, and movements, and Black intellectual attempts to build a diverse, just, and equitable society.
objectives: Explain and evaluate the basic principles of African philosophy.
Identify and analyze elements of African philosophy in the political, social, and cultural expressions of African and African American thinkers from earliest times to the present.
Examine and apply African and African American philosophical traditions to contemporary issues.
Analyze and assess historical data in anticipation of formulating creative and independent explanations for historical events and their relation to philosophical thought.
Formulate and defend alternative explanations and conclusions on the history and philosophy of African and African American thought.
Analyze African and African American thinkers’ critiques of the structures and consequences of imperialism, settler colonialism, and exploitation colonialism.
Examine intersections of race and racism with xenophobia, class, gender, sexuality, and ability in traditions of Black thought.
Evaluate cultural productions (literature, art, film, music) as sources of theory and knowledge in traditions of Black thought.
Define and explain the concept of intersectionality and its prominent place in African and African American philosophy and thought.
Investigate how religion, spirituality, and language intersect in the formation and articulation of Black thought and assess how they impact intellectual traditions.
Assess transnational and diasporic connections within traditions of Black thought.
Identify and compare key anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, anti-imperial, and Black feminist frameworks within African and African American philosophy and traditions of Black thought.
Evaluate the role of agency, identity formation, and group affirmation in Black thought as responses to Eurocentrism and white supremacy.

Examine how struggle, resistance, and solidarity in Black thought provide frameworks for understanding both historical movements and contemporary issues in the United States and across the African Diaspora.
Apply frameworks of Black thought to engage in praxis by connecting philosophical traditions to anti-racist, decolonial, and abolitionist movements for justice in contemporary society.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age, as experienced by Women of Color in Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina and Latino American communities.

Critically situate in historical context and review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Women of Color in Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina and Latino American communities, are relevant to current and structural issues at the local, national, international, and transnational levels. Such issues may be communal, national, international, and transnational politics, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial thought, issues, and the practices and movements as developed and led by Women of Color in Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina and Latino American communities toward a just and equitable society.
objectives: Introduce foundational concepts and frameworks such as race, racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, and eurocentrism as central to the study of Women of Color in the United States.

Examine systems of domination and resistance by analyzing white supremacy, anti-Blackness, imperialism, settler colonialism, and exploitation colonialism through the scholarship and activism of Women of Color.

Critically engage with womanist, feminist, and decolonial thought to understand how Women of Color conceptualize identity, oppression, and empowerment across historical and contemporary contexts.

Connect theoretical analysis to humanities traditions by studying philosophical, literary, aesthetic, and cultural works produced by Women of Color as expressions of survival, agency, and social transformation.
Introduce theoretical frameworks and knowledge traditions produced by Women of Color in Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina/o/x communities.
Examine critical events, histories, and cultural contributions to understand how Women of Color have shaped intellectual and social traditions in the United States.
Analyze processes of subjection and subject formation to reveal how systems of oppression construct identity and difference for Women of Color across multiple contexts.
Highlight agency and strategies of group affirmation by exploring how Women of Color create spaces for survival, empowerment, and solidarity.
Engage with literary, philosophical, aesthetic, and cultural works by Women of Color to critically appreciate their contributions to thought, art, spirituality, and activism.

Introduce the intersections of race and racism with class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and age in the lives of Women of Color.

Examine historical and contemporary experiences of oppression and resistance across Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina/o/x communities to reveal how intersecting systems of power operate.
Analyze womanist, feminist, and decolonial frameworks that illuminate how Women of Color theorize identity, subject formation, and collective empowerment within overlapping structures of domination.

Engage with philosophical, literary, aesthetic, and cultural works by Women of Color to critically assess how intersectional identities are expressed through intellectual traditions, artistic practices, and spiritual or communal worldviews.
Apply intersectional analysis to structural and current issues by exploring case studies and contemporary debates related to sovereignty, immigration, language policies, and social justice movements.
Introduce the historical contexts of struggle and resistance as experienced by Women of Color in Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina/o/x communities.
Examine movements for racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation led by Women of Color, situating them within broader histories of activism and intellectual traditions.

Analyze how historical struggles remain relevant to contemporary issues such as immigration, reparations, settler colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies at local, national, international, and transnational levels.
Critically engage with philosophical, literary, aesthetic, and cultural works produced by Women of Color that articulate strategies of survival, agency, and collective empowerment.
Evaluate the contributions of womanist and feminist frameworks to understanding how Women of Color theorize liberation and solidarity in response to structural oppression.
Connect theory and practice through applied learning by engaging in community-based or collaborative projects that link historical struggles with present-day social justice concerns.
Introduce anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial frameworks as articulated by Women of Color across Native American, African American, Asian American, and Latina/o/x communities.
Examine historical and contemporary practices and movements led by Women of Color that advance justice, equity, and liberation, with attention to cultural, philosophical, and literary contributions.
Analyze womanist, feminist, and decolonial perspectives to understand how Women of Color conceptualize solidarity, resistance, and collective empowerment.

Engage critically with works of intellectual, historical, and cultural importance—including scholarship, media, oral traditions, and creative expression—to appreciate how Women of Color shape movements for a just society.

Connect theory to practice through community engagement by reflecting on how the principles of anti-racism, abolition, anti-colonialism, and anti-imperialism inform both personal positionality and collective struggle.

Solve systems of equations and inequalities.
Apply functions to model real world applications.
Identify special triangles and their related angle and side measures.
Evaluate the trigonometric function of an angle given in degree and radian measure.
Manipulate and simplify a trigonometric expression.
Solve trigonometric equations, triangles, and applications.
Graph the basic trigonometric functions and apply changes in period, phase shift and amplitude to generate new graphs.
Prove trigonometric identities.
Solve and apply equations including rational, linear, polynomial, exponential, absolute value, radical, and logarithmic.
Solve linear, nonlinear and absolute value inequalities.
Graph the basic trigonometric functions and apply changes in period, phase shift and amplitude to generate new graphs.
Evaluate and graph inverse trigonometric functions.
Convert between polar and rectangular coordinates.
Calculate powers and roots of complex numbers using DeMoivre's Theorem.
Introduction to vectors.
Solve applications involving the Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles.
Solve applications involving angles and a transversal.
Solve applications involving the distance formula.
Solve applications involving similar triangles.
Find the area and volume of geometric shapes.

rows.title: Statistics for STEM
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Distinguish among standard methods of collecting data, use statistical software to summarize data numerically and visually, and interpret data.
Use programming to calculate measure of central tendency and variation for big data sets.
Compare and contrast the different types of distributions.

Compute confidence intervals and conduct hypothesis testing using parametric and/or nonparametric (for 1 and 2 populations) in applied settings. Make statistical conclusions using statistical software.
objectives: Use statistical software to interpret data numerically and visually with tables, charts, and graphs.
Calculate the probability of a given event using elementary probability techniques and the definition of sample space. Use probability to answer questions in the context of data.
Use algebraic methods and statistical software to calculate measures of central tendency and variation.
Differentiate between standard methods of data collection and identify limitations in data collection methods.
Use programming to calculate the mean and variance of a discrete distribution.
Demonstrate an understanding of the different types of distributions and be able to determine the appropriate distribution to calculate probabilities.
Implement Central Limit Theorem to understand phenomena.

Calculate and interpret confidence interval estimates of various parameters including single means and proportions as well as two population means and proportions. Justify the choice and confidence interval by demonstrating that the necessary criteria are met. Understand the effects of changing the confidence level of a confidence interval.
Interpret level of statistical significance using traditional method and p-values including an analysis of type I and II errors.
Use Python, R, or SAS to perform statistical analysis and be able to interpret the output.
Apply the basic concept of hypothesis testing to interpret level of statistical significance using traditional and p-values including an analysis of type I and II errors.

Perform parametric and non-parametric hypothesis tests including t-test for single and two population means, proportions, chi-square tests, and ANOVA. Interpret these results in context and justify the choice of test by demonstrating that the necessary criteria are met. Understand the effects of changing the significance level of a hypothesis test.
Use programming to analyze and interpret applications based on data from the following disciplines: life science, physical science, health science, information technology and STEM related majors.
Use regression lines and ANOVA for estimation and inference and interpret the associated statistics.
Complete a research project that employs simple statistical inference and advanced modeling techniques.

rows.title: Nursing Learning Laboratory
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: At the novice level, the student will: Provide quality, safe, patient-centered nursing care using evidence-based practices for healthy patients and those with specific alterations in health across the lifespan.

Integrate the scope and standards of practice of the professional nurse generalist, applying ethical and legal principles, when providing care to healthy patients and those with specific alterations in health.
Implement leadership principles in select healthcare settings for diverse patient populations.
Initiate caring behaviors that support relationship-centered care and demonstrate respect and sensitivity to others in preparation for becoming a competent, entry-level professional nurse generalist.

Initiate collaborative relationships using effective communication with the interprofessional health care team for the purpose of providing and improving patient outcomes in preparation for becoming a competent, entry-level professional nurse generalist.
Demonstrate critical thinking and clinical reasoning to form clinical judgments necessary for providing safe patient care and promoting quality improvement in a variety of health care settings.

Apply nursing informatics and technology to effectively communicate, enhance knowledge, manage and analyze data, prevent errors, and support decision-making when providing care for healthy patients and those with specific alterations in health.
objectives: At the novice level: Quality, Safe, Patient-Centered Care A. Develop and initiate a patient-centered plan of care, using the nursing process, that addresses the psychosocial and physiological needs for patients with chronic illness(es) across the lifespan and those with acute health care needs in a variety of health care systems. B. Perform and document an assessment of specific patient populations encompassing values, preferences, expressed needs, and the impact of developmental, emotional, cultural, religious, and spiritual influences on the patient’s health status. C. Select patient-centered health teaching interventions that address such topics as healthy lifestyles, risk-reducing behaviors, developmental needs, activities of daily living, and preventative self-care. D. Incorporate patient-centered care interventions that demonstrate sensitivity and respect for the diversity of the human experience. E. Use evidence-based practices to guide clinical decision-making in the delivery of quality, safe nursing care. F. Safely perform psychomotor nursing skills, as outlined in the Nursing Skills Across the Curriculum, within the context of the patient situation. G. Demonstrate patient advocacy skills in the care of assigned patients and their families.

Ethical and Legal Principles A. Incorporate professional standards, ethical behaviors, and legal principles of nursing practice. B. Support the image of nursing by modeling the values and articulating the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of the nursing profession. C. Demonstrate professional attitudes and behaviors, including attention to appearance, demeanor, respect for self and others, and attention to professional boundaries with patients and families as well as caregivers. D. Value the pursuit of practice excellence, lifelong learning, and engagement in activities that foster professional growth and development in preparation for becoming a professional nurse generalist.

Leadership Principles A. Implement organizational and time management skills to safely manage the health care needs of assigned patients. B. Begin to assume a leadership role as a member of the health care team in a variety of patient care settings. C. Demonstrate accountability and responsibility for nursing care provided and identify situations when care can be delegated, in a variety of health care settings, to other members of the health care team. D. Explain quality improvement principles and processes to effectively implement patient safety initiatives and how they contribute to improving patient care outcomes.

Caring A. Incorporate interventions to address patient and family needs that include input from other health care team members when planning or providing patient-centered care. B. Implement nursing interventions appropriate to the patient’s developmental level; physical and psychological needs; spiritual beliefs; and culture. C. Plan nursing care to facilitate the achievement of expected patient outcomes in a collaborative and caring manner that provides direction for continuity of care. D. Incorporate relationship-centered care principles when caring for self and interacting with patients, families, peers, and other members of the health care team.

Collaborative Relationships A. Incorporate effective communication techniques to foster positive professional working relationships. B. Foster collaborative relationships with the health care team, using appropriate communication skills, to improve patient outcomes and ensure the delivery of evidence-based patient-centered care. C. Select and perform interventions that promote quality, safe patient-centered care as a member of the health care team that contributes to improving patient care outcomes. D. Summarize and document patient care data to inform the health care team and contribute to clinical decision-making. E. Summarize and report relevant information to an appropriate health care team member to improve patient outcomes.

Critical Thinking A. Demonstrate clinical reasoning and judgment skills in providing quality, safe patient-centered care to assigned patients. B. Collect data, identify problems, establish goals, and select interventions based on the patient’s immediate or anticipated needs of the patient and situation. C. Perform ongoing evaluation of expected outcomes and interventions for assigned patients and revise the individualized plan of care as needed. D. Participate in self-reflection strategies to identify professional learning needs. E. Incorporate quality improvement activities to identify and prevent potential problems that may interfere with the delivery of safe patient care in a variety of health care settings.

Nursing Informatics A. Demonstrate computer literacy, including the ability to use desktop applications and mobile technology to promote effective communication and support decision-making. B. Competently use patient care technologies, information systems, and mobile technology to support safe nursing care for assigned patients in a variety of health care settings. C. Demonstrate the use of information technology systems to prevent the risk of errors and improve clinical outcomes in the delivery of safe patient care. D. Access data and documents using the nursing process via electronic health record, abiding by all ethical and legal standards.

Leadership: A. Caring A. Collaboration: A. Integrate and adapt effective communication techniques to foster positive professional working relationships. B. Contribute the unique nursing perspective when collaborating with the health care team, adapting communication skills as needed, to improve patient outcomes and ensure the delivery of evidence-based patient-centered care. C. D. Analyze, prioritize, and document patient care data to inform the interprofessional health care team and contribute to clinical decision-making in preparation for becoming a competent, entry-level professional nurse generalist. E. Prioritize and report relevant information to an appropriate interprofessional health care team member to improve patient outcomes.

Critical Thinking: A. Justify clinical reasoning and judgment skills when providing quality, safe patient-centered care to assigned patients. B. Individualize data collection, prioritize problems, establish goals, and plan comprehensive interventions for patients with complex health care needs across the lifespan based on the assessed immediate or anticipated needs. C. Monitor, analyze, and adapt nursing care, as needed, based on ongoing evaluation data for patients with complex alterations in health across the lifespan. D. Engage in self-reflection and inquiry to assume the role of a competent, entry-level professional nurse generalist. E. Execute quality improvement activities to prevent potential problems that may interfere with the delivery of safe patient care in a variety of health care settings.

Informatics: A. Demonstrate computer skills and mobile technology to promote effective communication and support decision-making. B. Competently use patient care technologies, information systems, and mobile technology to support safe nursing care for patients with complex alterations in health across the lifespan in a variety of health care settings. C. Competently use information technology systems to prevent the risk of errors and improve clinical outcomes in the delivery of safe patient care. D. Access relevant data and competently document using the nursing process via electronic health record, abiding by all ethical and legal standards.

rows.title: Honors Race and Ethnic Relations
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of concepts and classical and contemporary theoretical explanations of race and ethnic relations in the social sciences and analyze and articulate concepts of ethnic studies, including but not limited to race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, prejudice, stereotyping, discrimination, racism and anti-racism.

Critically discuss the intersection of race and ethnicity with other forms of difference affected by hierarchy and oppression, such as class, gender, sexuality, ability, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, and age as sources of intergroup conflict.

Demonstrate knowledge and apply theory of the history and contemporary status of racial and ethnic minority groups in the United States, with special focus on the lived-experiences and social struggles of historically defined racialized core groups: Indigenous/Native, Black/African Americans, Latinx, Asian, Pacific Islanders and/or Middle Eastern Americans and emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.

Demonstrate the ability to think critically, provide a critical analysis, and make content relevant to current issues of foreign and domestic systems of race and ethnic relations in a manner to understand their causes and consequences.
Describe possible remedies for local, national, and global inequalities, with a focus on struggles, resistance, social justice, solidarity and liberation as experienced by communities of color.
Demonstrate active engagement with anti-racist issues, practices and movements to build a diverse, just and equitable society beyond the classroom.
objectives: Recognize systems of institutional racism and discrimination.
Understand the relationship and potential for conflict between the majority group ad minority groups in a society.
Analyze patterns of migration and immigration as they relate to social change regarding race and ethnicity.

rows.title: Spanish 3
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate reading and listening comprehension of the substance of (a) standard discourse on familiar topics and (b) clearly-delivered authentic cultural materials. These may include, but are not limited to TV programs, videos, movies, audio files, Internet sources and literary and factual texts which put forward arguments and different points of view.

Formulate and express opinions, both orally and in writing, on familiar matters as well as on topics related but not limited to problems of an urban society, immigration, ecology, geography, and current events. This communication may include, but is not limited to, intermediate-level verbal exchanges and short essays that put forward personal points of view.

Reflect on and evaluate similarities and differences in cultural practices, values, norms, customs, events and perspectives as related, but not limited to, shopping, bargaining, the metric system, values, giving advice, expressing reactions, stereotypes, lifestyles and pastimes.
objectives: Apply listening strategies to comprehend standard spoken Spanish related to familiar topics, values, advice, surviving in a foreign culture, geography, history and pastimes with a recognition vocabulary of approximately 3000 words.

Synthesize acquired grammar and vocabulary to understand the gist of authentic Spanish-language cultural materials delivered through multimedia when the topics are familiar or related to content such as, but not limited to travel, gastronomy, customs, the metric system, social organizations, elections, geography, history and lifestyles.

Apply reading strategies in order to understand and evaluate 300- to 400-word literary and cultural texts that present not only factual content but also diverse opinions and analyses of topics such as, but not limited to, current events and issues that reflect socioeconomic changes.

Use knowledge of the indicative mood (simple present, present progressive, preterit, imperfect, perfect, conditional and future tenses) to understand readings that target present and past experiences as well as future plans and conditions.
Apply knowledge of the subjunctive mood (present and imperfect) and formal commands to understand readings that present advice, suggestions and changes.
Apply speaking strategies to produce spoken Spanish using an active lexicon of approximately 1500 words on topics related to Hispanic culture, history, current events and daily life.

Synthesize acquired knowledge of target vocabulary and the indicative and subjunctive moods to formulate and express opinions and put forward personal points of view on familiar matters as well as on topics such as, but not limited to, stereotypes, values, religion, current events, elections and world view.
Apply writing strategies to compose written paragraphs of 200 to 300 words on topics related to Hispanic culture, history, current events and daily life.
Use analytical and critical thinking skills to compose short essays that put forward personal points of view, offer advice and compare and contrast cultural and historical themes.

Demonstrate awareness of similarities and differences between Spanish-speaking cultures and their own as related to traditions, customs, religious beliefs, daily life, attitudes, feelings, emotions, values, norms and perspectives.

Identify appropriate statistical techniques and use technology-based statistical analysis to describe, interpret, and communicate results. (CCN required)
Evaluate ethical issues in statistical practice. (CCN required)
